title: Matrix Builds
subtitle: Test across multiple Node versions, OS, and configurations in parallel with one job definition

content.text: A matrix build runs the same job multiple times with different values — simultaneously, in parallel. Instead of writing three separate jobs to test on Node 18, 20, and 22, you define one job with a matrix of three values and GitHub creates three parallel jobs automatically.

content.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20, 22]
      # fail-fast: false means all matrix jobs complete even if one fails
      # Good for finding ALL compatibility issues, not just the first
      fail-fast: false

    name: Test on Node ${{ matrix.node-version }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        node: [18, 20]
      # Creates 3 OS × 2 Node = 6 parallel jobs:
      # ubuntu-18, ubuntu-20, windows-18, windows-20, mac-18, mac-20

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [18, 20, 22]
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]

        # include: ADD extra jobs with additional properties
        include:
          # Run Node 20 on macOS too (not in the base matrix)
          - node: 20
            os: macos-latest
          # Add an extra env var only for Node 22 jobs
          - node: 22
            experimental: true

        # exclude: REMOVE specific combinations
        exclude:
          # Skip Node 18 on Windows
          - node: 18
            os: windows-latest

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

    # Mark experimental jobs so failure doesn't fail the whole workflow
    continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '${{ matrix.node }}' }
      - run: npm ci && npm test

content.text: Keep matrices focused. A 3×3×3 matrix = 27 parallel jobs. Each uses CI minutes and contributes to runner queue wait time. For most projects, testing on the LTS Node version on Ubuntu is sufficient for PRs, with a broader matrix on release branches. Don't matrix for the sake of it.

questions.question: A matrix job has node: [18, 20] and os: [ubuntu, windows, macos]. fail-fast: true (default). The Node 18 + Windows job fails. What happens?
options: All 6 jobs finish — fail-fast only affects sequential jobs
The remaining in-progress jobs continue, but no new matrix jobs start. The job reports failure.
GitHub immediately cancels all 5 remaining matrix jobs
Only the failed job is re-run automatically
questions.explanation: With fail-fast: true (the default), when any matrix job fails: GitHub cancels all jobs that haven't started yet, but lets already-running jobs finish. Then the whole matrix job reports failure. With fail-fast: false, ALL matrix jobs run to completion regardless of failures — useful to see all failing combinations at once.

faq.q: Can I use a matrix for deployment targets?
faq.a: Yes — matrix: environment: [staging, eu-west, us-east] lets you deploy to multiple regions in parallel. Combine with environment protection rules to require approval for each. This pattern is common for multi-region global deployments.

examples: Every major npm package (express, lodash, zod) tests against multiple Node.js versions in CI to guarantee compatibility before publishing
Electron apps test on Windows, macOS, and Linux in matrix builds — native code behaves differently on each OS
